text: 10 episodes of a system that reads earnings calls and scores what executives said. This week it starts scoring what they didn't. I'm Anjana, and the most interesting signal on a call turns out to be the question that never got a straight answer. ASIS extracts financial guidance signals from earnings call transcripts using four readers: Keyword, FinBERT, NER, and LLM triangulated with dynamic weights. A prediction layer forecasts next quarter direction with pre-registered graded predictions. Episode 10 added the business analytics layer. Sector sentiment aggregation, a mood index, cross-sector heat maps, management confidence scoring, CEO CFO tone divergence, signal to price correlation ranking, surprise score analytics, and reaction window curves. Now, in episode

11, the system learns to detect when executives dodge questions, track competitive positioning language, and predict guidance revisions. Earnings calls have a Q and a section where analysts press management for answers. The system now parses every question-answer pair, classifying questions as forward-looking, backward-looking, clarification, or confrontational. A Crossing Coda reranker scores how directly each answer addresses its question, not just semantic similarity, but actual relevance. The dodge score is weighted by question importance. Evading a confrontational question about margin scores higher than sidestepping a clarification. Per speaker and per call dodge scores are tracked across quarters. How a company talks about competition reveals strategy. Three classifiers work together. A lexicon-based scorer matches

Phrases like gaining share or defending margins. A zero-shot classifier using BART handles novel phrasing the lexicon misses, and a fine-tuned stance detection model captures subtler positioning. The ensemble scores each call on an offensive to defensive spectrum. A tracking module monitors shifts across quarters. When a company flips from offensive to defensive language, the system flags it. Can the system predict whether a company will revise its guidance next quarter? A feature vector combines hedging index, management confidence, guidance specificity change, CEO CFO divergence, dodge score, market share language shift, forward-looking density delta, sentiment delta, and sector mood positioning. Six models compete. Logistic regression for interpretability, XG boost and light

GBM for gradient boosting, random forest for variance reduction, a small neural network for non-linear interactions, and cat boost for native categorical handling. All evaluated with time-aware cross-validation, bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired permutation tests to upgrade strengthen the foundation under all analytics. First, sentence BERT was fine-tuned on financial earnings call Q and appears, replacing generic embeddings with domain-specific representations that improve retrieval quality across dodge scoring, similarity matching, and feature engineering. Second, a FinBERT ensemble runs multiple checkpoints and averages predictions, reducing the variance that comes from relying on a single checkpoint. More stable sentiment scores feed into every downstream module. Dodge detection, competitive positioning, guidance revision prediction, stronger

Embeddings. The system now reads not just what executives say, but what they avoid saying. ASIS episode 11, reading between the questions. Let's recap with Claude. 10 episodes built a system that scores what was said. This one scores what was avoided. Every question and answer pair gets a relevant score from a cross encoder. How directly the answer addresses the question, which is not the same thing as how similar they are. Dodges are weighted by what was being dodged. How a company talks about competition lands on an offensive to defensive spectrum, and a flip across quarters gets flagged. And nine behavioral features feed six competing models that try to predict next

Quarter's guidance revision. None of which is worth much on a weak foundation. So, the embeddings underneath got retrained, too. Your turn. Here's the move worth stealing. Most of us score what people said and never score what they didn't. Take somewhere you already have questions and answers side by side. Support tickets, user interviews, performance reviews, and ask whether the answers actually address the questions or merely sit near them. Paste this into Claude and read the third part of its answer hardest, because that's the one that tells you whether you've been measuring evasion or just measuring politeness. And Jonna here, thanks for watching.
